### Exact wording

English (as recorded here)

“Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions.”

English

“Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions, and can never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.”

The archive quotes the first clause; Hume's full sentence adds the office reason may claim. Cutting the second half makes the claim sound wilder than the paragraph argues.

#### Forms in circulation that differ

-   “Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions.”
-   “Reason is the slave of the passions.”

### Attribution notes

Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature II.3.3. He is denying that reason alone can motivate action, not recommending passion over thought. The truncated “reason is the slave of the passions” is the version that circulates as a slogan against rationality.

#### About David Hume

David Hume (1711–1776) was the Scottish Enlightenment’s greatest empiricist and skeptical naturalist, author of the Treatise of Human Nature and later Enquiries. Largely denied academic chairs over religious suspicion, he served as librarian and diplomat and wrote a bestselling History of England.

### Interpretation

Hume's sentence reverses the usual hierarchy in which reason governs passion. His argument in the Treatise is that reason alone cannot initiate action because it deals in relations of ideas and matters of fact, neither of which contains a motive. Motivation comes from desire or aversion; reason's job is to work out means and to correct factual errors about them. Calling reason the slave of the passions is deliberately shocking, but the claim is structural rather than a recommendation to stop thinking.

#### Why it matters

It explains why argument alone rarely changes anyone's mind. If a belief is held because it serves a desire, the productive question is what that desire is — not what further evidence might be supplied.

### Questions readers arrive with

#### What is the source of the quotation “Reason is, and ought only to be the…”?

“Reason is, and ought only to be the…” comes from Treatise, II.3.3, attributed to David Hume.

#### What does David Hume mean by reason?

Philosophers disagree about whether reason is the slave of the passions, the legislator of morality, or one tool among others. The quotations here keep that disagreement in play. This passage enters that discussion through reason, desire.

#### Is the wording of this David Hume quotation commonly changed?

The wording recorded here is “Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions.” Forms in circulation that differ: Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions. / Reason is the slave of the passions. The English reads “Reason is, and ought only to be the slave of the passions, and can never pretend to any other office than to serve and obey them.”

#### Is this quotation attributed correctly?

Hume, A Treatise of Human Nature II.3.3. He is denying that reason alone can motivate action, not recommending passion over thought. The truncated “reason is the slave of the passions” is the version that circulates as a slogan against rationality.
